Question: Do earthquakes have an equivalent for exoplanets?
Answer: Yes, an exoplanet with tectonic activity is discovered, the LHS 3844b located 45 light-years from Earth. Image: Scientists from the University of Bern discovered the material inside LHS 3844b flows from one hemisphere to the other causing volcanic and tectonic activity. The truth is that we would expect quakes to occur on any rocky planet (the biggest magnitude of Marsquake recorded was 5 R). The causes may vary: 1. Pulsating Quakes. This type of quake occurs on a planet with a dense atmosphere. The atmosphere causes the crust of the planet to expand and contract. The pressure changes when this happens, causing the crust to crack and rebound. If the cracks become too large, they can lead to a pulsating quake. 2. Rotational Quakes. A planet's rotation may cause its crust to bulge outwards. This creates tension between the upper and lower layers of the planet's crust. As the planet rotates, the stress increases until it becomes strong enough to rupture the rock. This leads to a rotational quake. 3. Tectonic Shaking. Tectonic shaking is similar to rotational oscillation except that it does not involve the entire planet. Instead, tectonic vibration only affects certain areas of the planet. It is believed that tectonic shaking occurs when two plates collide. One plate slides under another, creating friction. Friction heats the plates, which eventually breaks them apart. Once the plates separate, the resulting shock wave travels through the planet's mantle. 4. Volcanic Shaking. Volcanoes are one of the best ways for an object to lose heat. They create hot lava flows that travel through the planet's interior. When the lava hits the mantle, it produces a volcanic shake. 5. Crustal Shaking. Crustal shaking occurs when the top layer of the planet s crust moves relative to the underlying mantle. This movement causes the veil to vibrate, which results in a seismic event. That is, no matter where you are in the Universe, avoid tall buildings. footnotes

Question: What made Alexander original and etc and great general and changed the world, history and Greece if Cyprus the Great did the same thing and Alexander copied him?
Answer: That wasn’t the case, Alexander didn’t copy Cyrus the Great (Cyprus is an island, not a Persian king). Cyrus and the Persian kings after him followed practically the same tactic as other great Asian conquerors before him (like the Hittites, for instance): He let his vassal regions do what they liked with only two but huge obligations; pay taxes to him and provide military personnel on his request. In return, he let them live. That meant in practice that the occupied regions (Ionian Greeks, Phoenicians, Egyptians, etc) kept their distinctive culture but were frequently exhausted financially and the income of all ended in the Persian treasury (this is why from time to time they revolted). Alexander had a different policy. He treated the conquered peoples equally with the Macedonians being their king, not their conqueror. That is why he gave high-ranking positions to Persians, imposed mixed marriages, and mainly invested in the conquered regions. The money from the Persian treasury did not go to Aigai but was used for projects throughout his empire. The result was the movement of ideas and people, which created the cultural explosion of the Hellenistic period. Do you want to see the difference? This is the Hibis Temple, Kharga Oasis, Egypt, constructed during the Persian occupation of Egypt. It is mostly indistinguishable from that of preceding periods. This is the main tomb in the catacombs at Kom el Shoqafa, Alexandria, of the Early Roman period construction. We can see a stunning conversation between Hellenistic and Egyptian architecture with elements from both cultures. If the merging of two civilizations of this class is not an achievement deserving the title of “Great” what does it? .

Question: Was Medusa possibly the Minoan snake goddess?
Answer: This is a very interesting question in which…I can’t give a clear answer. Some academics (mostly in the early 20th century) claim there is a connection between the Minoan snake goddess and Medusa, the notorious mortal Gorgon of Greek mythology, with snakes and both protective powers as their connecting links. However, there are some dark spots. Snakes, which represent the cycles of life, the seasons, and immortality as it was thought to shed their skin indefinitely, appear in many Minoan artifacts as religious symbols but is the woman holding them a goddess? In the bronze figurine below, the woman with the (maybe) snakes on her head is a worshipper for sure as she is making the Minoan worship gesture of a facepalm. Minoan figurine, praying woman, 1600 – 1500 BC. Find from Troas, Asia Minor, Turkey. Antikensammlung Berlin, Ident. N. Misc. 8092, now in the Neues Museum Berlin. Image credit User:Zde - Wikimedia Commons To complicate things more, although the dominant theory wants the snake goddess as a kind of animal mistress connected with fertility and rebirth, there are different opinions on what the goddess represents with the discussion going on until now. Woman-bearing snakes disappeared for long from Greek art after the collapse of the Minoans. Before we meet the snakes-bearing Medusa, we find her in the 7th century BCE Theogony by Hesiod but…she is a monster and has no snakes! “And again, Ceto bore to Phorcys the fair-cheeked Graeae, sisters grey from their birth … and the Gorgons who dwell beyond glorious Ocean in the frontier land towards Night where are the clear-voiced Hesperides, Sthenno, and Euryale, and Medusa who suffered a woeful fate: she was mortal, but the two were undying and grew not old. With her lay the Dark-haired One [Poseidon] in a soft meadow amid spring flowers. And when Perseus cut off her head, there sprang forth great Chrysaor and the horse Pegasus…” Hesiod, Theogony, In 270, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White In the art of the same period, known as the Orientalizing period, Medusa made her first appearance. She is a Centaurine in this Cycladic relief amphora of 650 BCE (no snakes) Paris Musée du Louvre CA 795. Photo. Chuzeville © Musée du Louvre The snakes make their appearance a little later while she’s still a monster Medusa wearing the belt of the intertwined snakes, a fertility symbol, as depicted on the west pediment of the Temple of Artemis on the island of Corfu. Dated ~580 BCE. Image Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International Are the symbols in common hard evidence to support the connection between the two? In addition, Medusa is also connected with Levantine deities (she was often depicted bearing wings), the Egyptian Eye of Horus, and the Egyptian snake goddess, Wadjet. So, she is primordial and predates the Greeks but her exact origin is still unclear. footnotes 57: Medusa Up Close and Personal From Snake Goddess to Medusa Medusa, Apollo, and the Great Mother on JSTOR Minoan snake goddess figurines - Wikipedia

Question: Can you tell me about The Dance of Apollo and Dionysus?
Answer: It is a clever metaphor by Nietzsche in his work The Birth of Tragedy to prove that the Greek tragedy was the only point in history when two opposing tensions, the “Apollonian” and the “Dionysian” were brought together. In Greek mythology, Apollo was the god of light, protector of music, poetry, and prophecy. Honored in temples and oracles like the Delphi, he is sober, elegant, and eloquent. In Nietzsche’s book, he represents the reason. On the other hand, Dionysus was associated with death and rebirth, fertility, wine-making, ritual madness. To accompany Dionysus was not an easy thing; the followers of Dionysus were both women and men, who are often depicted as mad and or intoxicated. He is the “irrational”. The dance of the Bacchants, by Charles Gleyre, 1849, via Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts, Lausanne The Birth of Tragedy is an essay on aesthetics. One of the book’s main premises is that “only as an aesthetic phenomenon is an existence and the world eternally justified”. Nietzschean philosophy traditionally sees existence as pain and chaos. Only art can make this pain bearable and Nietzsche finds that there are two artistic paths within art, the Apollonian and the Dionysian. After exploring them thoroughly, he concludes that the Greek tragedy was the only point in history when these two opposing tensions were brought together. For Nietzsche, Apollo is a deity related to calmness and reason. Dionysus is the god who embodies the experience of the drunken reality. Based on illusions or misrepresentations, drunken reality is instinctive. Unlike the structured, ordered illusion of the dream, drunkenness is deeply emotional and irrational. Within this chaotic reality, the subject is dissolved, becoming one with its surroundings. As a result, drunkenness is an experience of oneness or as Nietzsche calls it primordial unity. Theatre evolved out of the dithyramb, a ritual hymn including dancing, in honor of Dionysus. Thespis was the first person in history to step out of the dithyramb’s singularity. He began speaking in verse as an individual and representing a certain character. This was the birth of tragedy. Due to this special origin story, the ancient Greek tragedy was always a combination of epic and lyric poetry. Photo from Euripides' Bacchae directed by Alexis Minotis. Βάκχες του Ευριπίδη, μια από τις πιο αινιγματικές τραγωδίες της αρχαιοελληνικής γραμματείας | LiFO In the dithyramb, Nietzsche’s philosophy saw a purely Dionysian endeavor. Thespis’ stepping out of the dithyramb to embody a certain character was a process of individuation and, as a result, an Apollonian intrusion. Consequently, the Greek tragedy was born out of the fusion or rather the dialectic synthesis of the Apollonian and the Dionysian. Question: Is Greece the oldest democracy in the world/where democracy began?
Answer: The oldest recorded democracy was the Athenian one which reached its peak as a direct democracy by the late 4th century BCE. Question: What was the reason for the presence of many foreigners in Ancient Greece and Rome?
Answer: People in antiquity migrated for the same reasons as today, better work opportunities or seeking political asylum. Now, the rest of the question is totally wrong! During the archaic and classical periods, the ancient Greek city-states (ancient Greece was not one state) didn’t attract many foreigners. In addition, there were a lot of Greek cities outside of the Greek peninsula. Some exceptions were the rich ones among them such as Athens (most of the time), Corinth, or Syracuse, where mainly artisans and philosophers could find a larger audience or clientele. However, at the same time, Egypt attracted way more foreigners, only the Greek trade station of Heracleion and the colony of Naucratis counted more than 15,000 people, and if we count the Phoenician traders and the mercenaries in Egypt, the number of foreigners goes very high. Since the Hellenistic period, when travel became easier and the strict rules about foreigners loosened in most cities, people sought a better life abroad more frequently. Then again, the Hellenistic cities such as Alexandria, Pergamon, and Antioch were the most popular destinations. Rome did attract foreigners for the reasons mentioned above.

Question: What makes the Pergamon Ancient Greek Theatre unique, and what is its seating capacity and angle, distinguishing it in history?
Answer: It is a Hellenistic theatre, built on the steep west slope of the upper Acropolis of Pergamon. It was constructed in the 3rd century BCE, at the beginning of the Attalid dynasty, and renovated extensively by King Eumenes II (97-159 BCE). A marble stage house, a royal box, and a 246.5 meter-long, 17.4 meter-wide Doric colonnaded terrace (where the path is visible on the right of the photo below), the longest stoa in the Hellenistic world, were added later. The theater and a Byzantine tower. Image from Acropolis theatre of Pergamon The theatre may have had a seating capacity of 10,000 (the exact estimation is not possible) and the cavea (seating area) was the steepest in the ancient world (~70 degrees). The 80 rows of seats were arranged on three levels, divided by 3 walkways (diazomata) around the width of the cavea. At the front of the second row in the center of the cavea are the remains of the royal box. the royal box, image from Acropolis theatre of Pergamon The orchestra (stage) was a wooden construction that could be removed when not in use, to clear the terrace and the approach to the Temple of Dionysus at its north end. Today, all that remains of the monumental terrace is a footpath (on the right of the photo above), along which lie some of the fragments of the stoa (colonnade). It was replaced by a marble one in the 1st century BCE. Due to the limitations of the steep hillside site, the cavea could not be built wider than a semi-circle as in other Greek theatres, making the construction unique in the Hellenistic world. It was extended upwards to 37 meters above the orchestra and it was wise to watch your step…. footnotes Acropolis theatre of Pergamon ancient theatre of Pergamon

Question: Why do rainbows always have the shape of half circle & full circle rather than other fractions of a circle? Equating a rainbow to sine waves, what is a negative rainbow?
Answer: Rainbows have a curved shape because they’re made from light reflected after hitting spherical raindrops. And, of course, they can appear as another fraction of a circle as it is an optical phenomenon, it doesn’t really exist! Image credit: Rainbow at the end of 2015 Tucson AZ monsoon season A rainbow is a collection of rays from glinting raindrops that happen to reach our eyes. Raindrops glint rainbow rays at an angle of 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the sun. All the drops glinting in the rainbow are on the surface of a cone with its point at your eye. Other drops not on the cone also glint sunlight into rainbow colors but their rays do not reach our eyes. We only see those on the cone. When you look down the cone you see a circle. So rainbows are circles! from EPOD - a service of USRA . Photographer: Daniel Herron Summary Authors: Daniel Herron; Jim Foster The colorful set of curving stripes shown above may look like a halo but it's really a rainbow. On approach to Munich, our plane passed through a light rain shower. As we turned to land the Sun was positioned directly behind us, and this amazing rainbow magically appeared. Actually, all rainbows are circular. However, when we're stuck on the ground we're limited to seeing only the familiar arch and so assume that rainbows stop at the horizon. It was realized by Rene Descartes in the 1600s that a primary rainbow is a complete circle with a radius of approximately 42 degrees -- the minimum deviation angle of sunlight passing through raindrops. Despot, it is right for me to tell you my opinion as I think about what is best for you. This is my advice for you: don't fight at sea. Question: Were the Etruscans the descendants of the Minoans? Their appearance and culture appears so similar.
Answer: The evidence provided by genetics, historical studies, and archaeology says no! The genetic footprint of the Etruscans indicates that they are indigenous to Northwestern Italy (mainly Villanovan), while the Minoans are primarily Anatolian Farmers. The Minoan was a Bronze Age civilization, whereas the Etruscans appeared after 1000 BCE. There is no evidence of Minoan colonies in Italy, nor traces of a massive migration of Cretans after the collapse of the Bronze Age. So, if the Minoans were not the Etruscans’ forefathers how comes the similarity in their appearance and culture? We have to keep in mind that art depictions are not photos. They were both Mediterranean people with dark hair and brown eyes but this doesn’t make them similar and by no means the same! We can distinguish a modern Cretan and an inhabitant of Tuscany, can’t we? In addition, their cultures differed a lot; they had different languages (although none is deciphered), writing systems, burial customs, and religion…had the Minoans been there, something of their customs must have survived (like in Greeks and Mycenaeans). Nothing! In addition, Etruscan art is influenced by Greek one while keeping Villanovan elements. Judge by yourself: Etruscan fresco 5th century BCE (oops, the man in the middle is blond). Question: What was it like to be a Greek living under Roman rule?
Answer: The Greek lifestyle didn’t change much superficially. The clever Romans left seemingly untouched most of the Greek institutions (citizen’s assembly, Voule, etc) giving them the illusion they were still decided for their affairs. That wasn’t true, their decisions had to be under Roman law and they had to worship the Emperor, a new kind of relationship between a citizen and the ruler for most of them. By the time of Constantine the Great, the democratic institutions had become a caricature although the Assembly was never abandoned. Bronze statue of the Roman Emperor Augustus (27 BC – 14 AD); found in the Aegean Sea Creative Commons - Wikipedia They had to co-exist with Roman immigrants (or colonizers in some cases). Gradually, a lot of Roman habits passed in Greece, like the Roman spectacles of the arena—almost all the Greek theaters were altered so that they could host such games (only the theaters in Epidaurus and Larissa kept the original architecture). The theater, already of lower quality than the classical period, declined even more becoming a cheap spectacle. The Roman architecture succeeded the Hellenistic one in public and private constructions. Roman ruins in Athens gus619USA's User Profile | Atlas Obscura A lot of specialized Greeks (doctors, artists, architects, etc) migrated to Italy as the demand for Greek artifacts and services increased there. However, very few Greeks ever reached high-ranked offices of the Roman regime. Sarcophagus with a Greek Physician | Roman | The Metropolitan Museum of Art It was a mutual trade of culture that ended in many Greek customs adapted by the Romans (the Roman colonizers were totally Hellenized) and the Romanizing of the Greeks. Were the Greeks happy under the Roman rule? Yes, in a way. The Pax Romana and the wealth that followed it made them finally accept the Romans although they always felt the bitterness that their rulers were less civilized than themselves. This bitterness grew when Christianity prevailed in the empire. Greek was thought as a synonym for pagan and scorned for this.

Question: Was it illegal to be an atheist in ancient Rome or Greece?
Answer: It depends on the period. Theoretically, theism was the fundamental belief and any atheist person might be prosecuted, with atheism or impiety being capital crimes. In practice, the Greek societies were resilient to atheism although not fond of it. However, when the Greek philosophers back in the 6th century attempted to explain the world in a rational way instead of through religious myths, the first criticism of religion emerged. Xenophanes (6th century), for instance, wrote: If cows and horses had hands, then horses would draw the forms of gods like horses and cows like cows. Recorded by Clement of Alexandria in his work “Stromata”. Many philosophers, sophists, and poets like Anaxagoras, Leucippus, Democritus, the Epicureans, Aristophanes, and more expressed similar theories with only a few recorded prosecutions. In the most infamous case —the prosecution and conviction of Socrates in Athens— the true motive was political. Diagoras of Melos and Critias, a detail of the School of Athens by Raffaello Sanzio (1509). Both philosophers were considered atheists Although we can’t estimate the number of atheists during this period, there must be a small number as the philosophers mentioned had several followers. In the Imperial period, the state became much more severe, as doubting the gods equaled doubting the emperor (who was divine himself). This was the main reason for the execution of Christians. for further reading

Question: Why did Alexander the Great not conquer Sparta?
Answer: Alexander didn’t conquer any Greek city-state, why should he? Philip II, his father, created a Greek confederation allied against the Persians (the Corinthian League) in 340 BCE, with him being the military leader. Members of the alliance agreed never to attack each other except to suppress a revolt. Alexander inherited not only the Macedonian throne but the leadership of the Corinthian League too in which Sparta was not a member. He let it be as, just like his father, thought he had nothing to gain by forcing the Spartans to join the alliance. The alliance was strong enough without the Spartans who were too weak by then and incapable of becoming a serious threat. A note: Neither Philip nor Alexander conquered or occupied officially the city-states of the alliance. This changed later in the Hellenistic period. Alexander did take military action against Athens and Thebes because they revolted. Yet again, he didn’t enslave the cities.

Question: Why is Athens the only Greek city state we have texts from?
Answer: The statement that only Athenian texts survived to our days is completely false. A lot of the famous ancient Greek authors were not Athenians nor lived in Athens like Hesiod (from Askra, Boeotia), Archimedes (from Syracuse, Sicily), and Euclide (from Alexandria) to name just a few. Even some Athenian writers wrote their works away from Athens like Euripides who left Athens for Macedonia, after the invitation of King Archelaus. Maybe the impression that the Athenian writers dominated Greek literature derives from the popularity of Athenian philosophers like Plato or poets like Sophocles, all of them writers of the classical period. However, we must not forget that Greek literature was born in Asia Minor and the islands of the East Aegean, from where great philosophers like Thales and great poets like Sappho originated. In addition, the majority of the surviving Hellenistic texts were from the colonies or the Hellenistic kingdoms.

Question: Why didn't the ancient Greeks invent gravity?
Answer: Nobody has invented gravity. Gravity is the force, in a broader sense(*), of attraction between two or more masses anywhere in the Universe. It is a part of nature’s behavior which has existed before humanity and will be present after we’re gone. So, the ancient Greeks, or anyone else, couldn’t have invented it. However, the Greeks did try to explain it. Aristotle, for instance, claimed that objects fell towards the Earth because the Earth being the center of the Universe, attracted all of the mass in the Universe towards it (this claim has a tiny core of truth…) in Physics Book VIII. He also thought that the speed of a falling object should increase with its weight (this is completely wrong). In fact, they couldn’t do much better, they lacked the required mathematics. Newton, who actually studied gravity, had to invent it. (*) Space and time are not separate in the way we normally think, they are part of a combined concept called spacetime and, in addition, are not static. It changes (curves) in response to the presence of masses. This curving of spacetime is gravity. See below how it works: Massive bodies warp spacetime around them, leading the objects close to them to follow a curved path. Image credit: vchal via Getty Images For more: What is gravity?

Question: How does "The School of Athens" contribute to our understanding of Renaissance art and its relationship to classical philosophy?
Answer: School of Athens, Raphael, 1508-1512, Vatican Museum, Rome This big (8m x 4m) emblematic painting of the early Renaissance had an impact like few others, affecting both the aesthetic and philosophical approach of Renaissance painters. The depiction is purely secular (not a single saint or religious symbol is present in the painting), despite being commissioned by the Pope in an attempt to elevate the Church's authority in the tumultuous early years of the Renaissance. The brilliant Raphael uses allegories extensively (for example, the iconic staircase of the school symbolizing the step-by-step progress of science and the 'confrontation' of Plato with Aristotle representing the two different approaches in philosophy - the realistic, naturalistic one of Aristotle against the idealism of Plato). Of course, to appreciate and understand the allegories, knowledge of science, philosophy, and the lifestyle of classical antiquity is necessary. It seems that the intended audience was knowledgeable, and the painter was aware of it. However, do not expect historical accuracy in the painting; it does not exist. Many of those depicted (such as Euclid, Pythagoras, Ptolemy, or Hypatia) never set foot in Athens and certainly were never members of the School of Athens. But the artist's goal is not that anyway. The goal (to integrate pagan philosophers into the framework of Christianity) is fully achieved, simultaneously creating an aesthetic masterpiece. for more details about the painting:

Question: How does NASA study exoplanets (planets outside our solar system), and what have been some notable discoveries?
Answer: An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system orbiting other stars, but there are also free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, that orbit the galactic center and are untethered to any star. The first exoplanet, 51 Pegasi b, was discovered in 1995 by NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope. It is a hot, star-hugging gas giant believed to be about half the size of Jupiter. It tugged so hard on its parent star as it raced around in a four-day orbit that the star’s wobbling (keep this…) was obvious to earthly telescopes. Now, astronomers knew what to look for. 51 Pegasi b, also called "Dimidium," was the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a star like our sun. This groundbreaking find in 1995 confirmed planets like Earth could exist elsewhere in the universe. Credit: NASA (artistic presentation) A statistical estimate based on data from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope revealed that there are more planets than stars in our galaxy. That means there are more than a trillion planets in our galaxy alone, many of them in Earth’s size range. Up to now, more than 5,000 exoplanets have been discovered. How do we look for them? By reading the wobble of a star, that is, the change in its radial velocity; the wavelengths of starlight may appear alternately squeezed and stretched as a star moves slightly closer, then slightly farther away from us. Those gyrations are caused by gravitational tugs, this way and that, from orbiting planets. Then, spectroscopy is used to reveal the composition of the exoplanet. The color bands of its spectrum can be read like a bar code, revealing which molecules are present. Transit spectroscopy (light from a star travels through the atmosphere of an orbiting planet and reaches our telescopes) tells about where it's been. Gravitational microlensing takes advantage of an effect first described by Einstein: gravity's ability to warp and bend starlight. The gravity of a star in the foreground will magnify the light from a background star that passes just behind it. If the foreground star has a planet in orbit, the star will appear to a properly positioned telescope as a spike in light intensity as the background star goes by; the planet will appear as a second, smaller spike. Direct imaging, now available only for giant planets, it will be the next best thing…. A team of French astronomers used the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope to discover a giant exoplanet, Beta Pictoris b, resulting in this iconic direct image. Image credit: ESO/A.-M. Lagrange et al. Some notable discoveries: WASP-107b, a gas giant, orbiting a highly active K-type star about 200 light-years from Earth. Using spectroscopy, scientists detected helium escaping from the planet — the first time this element was found in an exoplanet atmosphere. Image credit: ESA/Hubble, NASA, M. Kornmesser Proxima Centauri b is our closest known exoplanet neighbor, at only 4 light-years away. It was discovered in 2016.
